defects.original:
They put the seed table in the square where people could approach it from any side. Sera refused the reeve's raised chair and used the bench normally reserved for repairing baskets. A person ought to be able to leave without appearing to walk away from a throne. Fenn brought the case after the households had heard the terms in private. Fenn returned the seed case to Sera. Sera checked all eleven seeds with her and closed the lid again before anyone made an offering. Orin hung a small unpolished bell on the table's end. It could call for attention, but Sera told the gathering that silence would count as silence, never as consent. Mael stood among the other villagers without his ceremonial coat. The silver glove lay on the council table beside the signed account of what he had taken.

[noncontiguous passage]

Mael brought the warm page to Fenn with both hands empty. It had held the remembered reed whistle after the name was scraped away, preserving the gift as an unclaimed object instead of letting the giver decide what followed. The warm page returned the memory Mael had taken. Fenn read the restored lines and spoke the name she had refused to speak in the cistern. The child’s name belonged to the memory’s rightful giver. Sera had expected a dramatic change in the air. Instead the page cooled, and Fenn remembered a small mistake in the tune that she had not known she had forgotten. Fenn had believed silence would protect the child’s name, but silence had protected Mael instead. The restored name did not bring the child back, and nobody suggested spending a seed as if rain could do that. Fenn asked for a chair away from the table. Sera gave her one and left the next question unasked until the old woman looked up again.

[noncontiguous passage]

The old bronze bell remained in the village square. People walked around it on their way to the well, touching the rough place that had once been a cooking pot. Sera stood in the village square when the first new rain fell. The rain was slight enough that dust remained beneath the benches, and the old cistern would need more than a ceremony to fill. Beyond the roofs a cloud gathered over the western ridge. Sera could not know whether the distant cloud had been made by their seeds. A natural cloud and a seed-made shower could occupy the same sky without announcing their origins to an apprentice. She wrote where the rain had first touched the square, because she had seen that. She did not draw a border around the cloud and claim it as the village's work. Mael watched her leave the line unfinished. For once he did not offer to finish it with a confident explanation.

[noncontiguous passage]

The clerk brought the new allotment book for her signature. She intended to teach the next apprentice to keep a written account. She wanted the next child entrusted with the case to know that a quantity could increase by a corrected count, decrease through an opened seed, and remain unchanged by a wish. If every gift remained voluntary, the orchard might never demand another debt. It was a hope about the future, not a weather report or a guarantee that nobody would deceive a giver again. The clerk wrote the conditional form as she spoke it. Fenn looked over the page and asked for a larger space beside the word declined. People should be able to refuse in more than a narrow margin. Sera drew the column wider and copied the page again, though it meant admitting the first neat version had been insufficient. The abandoned sheet became a cover for the seedlings instead of a record anyone had to defend.
